storySpine.obstacle: The graves have been closed and the valley floor is being levelled and paved as a public space.

changed: The source's archaeological and legendary material was reordered around an imagined scene, and the summary, details and story prose were written for this draft. The wording and the invented character are ours.
storyNote: The wall on the Palatine, the graves and paving in the valley, the shared offerings, and the joining of the hill villages come from the archaeological record. Vibia and her walk are invented. Romulus, Remus and the she-wolf belong to legend, and the scene never presents them as fact.
summary: Rome began as several villages on the hills beside the Tiber. Over the centuries they grew into one town, with a wall around its first hill and a shared meeting place in the valley below. Later Romans told a different story: that a man named Romulus founded the city in 753 BC, and that he and his twin Remus had been raised by a she-wolf. Most modern historians treat that story as myth.
details: Ancient writers gave Rome many different founding years. The earliest placed it around 1100 BC, in the age of the Trojan War, and Varro's date of 753 BC eventually became the standard. The Parilia, held on 21 April, commemorated the founding. The legend said the twins quarrelled and Remus was murdered. Modern scholars dismiss most of these accounts as myths, and the name Romulus itself is thought to come from the city's name.
story:
This scene is imagined. It takes place on the Palatine, one of the hills above the Tiber, in the years when the separate villages there were becoming a single town. The hill and the valley below it are real places, and the objects found in their ground are real. Vibia is not.

Vibia was ten. Her grandmother had died in the winter, and the family had laid her in the ground down in the valley. That valley held the graves of the hill people, and it had held them for a very long time. The graves there went back hundreds of years, generation after generation.

Now the valley was changing. Men were cutting the ground flat, and the old graves were being covered over with a hard surface of packed stone. Burials there had stopped, and the dead were not to be brought there any more.

Vibia carried a small pot down the hill, and it held a little grain saved from the last of the harvest. She wanted to set it at her grandmother's grave, because she had not been able to say goodbye.

At the edge of the valley she stopped. The ground was flat and hard, and she could not find the place where her grandmother lay. A man told her the graves were not to be used now, because the open space belonged to everyone.

She stood with the pot in her hands. The valley was busier than she had ever seen it, and people were coming down from all the hills around her. Some came from the Capitoline, which she knew, and others came from places she had never walked.

Then she saw the offerings. People had set small gifts in a low place at the centre of the valley. There were pots, and little figures, and food. The gifts were not for one family; they were for the town, and for all the hills that made it.

Vibia set her pot with the others. She stood there a moment, then turned back up the hill.

On the hill a wall had gone up. It was new, and it followed the edge of the hill all the way round. Vibia had watched the men set the stones the summer before, and she had thought then that it was only a fence.

There was a gate in the wall, and people passed through it both ways. Vibia saw that the wall did not shut the hills apart; it drew one line around all of them together. She went home through the gate, and she understood a little of what was happening.

claims.text: Rome grew from several hilltop villages that gradually united.
claims.quote: Rome developed from the gradual union of several hilltop villages

claims.text: By 1000 BC the Forum valley held a necropolis of cremation graves.
claims.quote: By 1000 BC, a necropolis existed in the Forum for cremation graves.

claims.text: Four major settlements emerged, on the Palatine, the Capitoline, the Quirinal and Viminal, and the Caelian, Oppian and Velia.
claims.quote: The nuclei appeared on the Palatine, the Capitoline, the Quirinal and Viminal, and the Caelian, Oppian, and Velia.

claims.text: The Forum was turned into a public space; burials stopped and parts were paved.
claims.quote: The area of the Forum also was converted at this time into a public space. Burials there discontinued and portions of it were paved over.

claims.text: Votive offerings appeared in the comitium in the eighth century, showing a more central cult.
claims.quote: Votive offerings appear in the comitium in the eighth century, indicating a more central religious cult

claims.text: The first wall on the Palatine is dated between 730 and 720 BC.
claims.quote: The first evidence of a wall appears in the middle or late eighth century on the Palatine, dated between 730 and 720 BC.

claims.text: The wall may have marked the boundary later Romans called the pomerium.
claims.quote: It is possible that the circuit of the wall marked out what later Romans believed to be the original pomerium

claims.text: Gates and streets were found connected to the wall.
claims.quote: The discovery of gates and streets connected to the wall

claims.text: The hilltop settlements combined into a single polity by the later eighth century BC.
claims.quote: The combination of the hilltop settlements into a single polity by the later 8th century BC

claims.text: The Parilia festival on 21 April commemorated the founding of the city.
